statement: In people who use heroin, evidence is insufficient to say whether taking it in surroundings not linked with past use raises the risk of overdose: the idea comes from a conditioning model of tolerance tested mainly in rats, and the only study in people is a set of 10 overdose survivors' recollections with no comparison. The model, as its author states it (Siegel, 1984, 2005): cues present when a drug is taken, such as the place, the people and the act of taking it, become linked with its effects and come to trigger responses that oppose those effects; these learned responses are part of tolerance, so tolerance should be weaker where the drug has not been taken before. The animal evidence is described by the same author without figures: rats with the same heroin history were more likely to survive a high intravenous dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin than the same dose given in a different environment (Siegel et al., 1982, as described in Siegel, 1984; the 1982 paper itself was not read), and setting-specific tolerance is said to have been seen for a variety of effects, lethal effects included, of various drugs in many species (Siegel, 2005, citing his group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure named). The 2005 review also describes, without numbers, two laboratory examples in people that do not involve opioids: more tolerance to alcohol drunk in a familiar beer-flavoured drink than in an unfamiliar blue, peppermint-flavoured one, and more tolerance to a heart effect of caffeine taken in coffee than at the same blood level reached intravenously. The only human study of overdose: 10 people formerly dependent on heroin (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28), attending one methadone maintenance clinic in the New York City area and each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records, were asked to recount the occasion on average 5 years later; 7 described something unusual: 2 had injected in places where they had never injected before, 1 had used for the first time in his own living room, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply, 2 described an unusual injection, 1 had taken a barbiturate mixture with the heroin against his usual practice, and 1 had injected heroin without the cocaine he usually took with it; 3 recalled nothing distinctive (Siegel, 1984). An unfamiliar place or company was thus recalled by 3 of the 10 (editors' count). There was no comparison with these people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose, the accounts were sorted by the author without stated definitions, and only survivors were interviewed, although the abstract extends the suggestion to overdose deaths; the author states that the reports do not prove a conditioning mechanism, that large doses and drug combinations also contribute, that the barbiturate case may be a drug interaction, and that how often people use heroin in unusual circumstances without harm is unknown. The 2005 review presents no data on overdose in people and does not cite the interviews; it proposes a form of cue-exposure treatment (meeting drug cues without the drug, so that the learned responses fade) that also includes internal cues, and cites no trial of it. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely? Maybe, but in people nobody has tested it properly. The idea comes from learning: the place, the people and the ritual that usually come with a drug start to trigger the body's own push-back against it, and that push-back is part of tolerance, so tolerance may be weaker somewhere new. In rat experiments by the researcher who proposed this, tolerance was weaker in an unfamiliar place, and a large dose of heroin was more often deadly there than in the usual place. The only study in people asked 10 overdose survivors in methadone treatment in New York, about 5 years later, what had been different that day. Seven recalled something unusual, but only 3 meant a new place or crowd; 2 meant a different way of injecting and 2 a different mix of drugs, and 3 recalled nothing unusual. Nobody compared these days with the same people's ordinary days, or counted how often people use somewhere new without overdosing, so the study can't show a higher risk. A treatment based on the idea was proposed without any trial.
population: People who use heroin: in the only human study, 10 people formerly dependent on heroin, in methadone maintenance at one clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28 at interview), interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; in the animal work the model's author describes, rats and other species
exposure: Taking an opioid in surroundings, company or circumstances not previously linked with taking it (in the human study, anything the person recalled as unusual on the overdose occasion: an unfamiliar place or company, an unusual injection, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usual one)
comparator: None in the human study (no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose); in the rat experiment, the same final dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin, to rats with the same heroin history
outcome: Overdose (hospital-treated, survivors only) in people; in animals, tolerance and death after a high dose
magnitude: Siegel (1984): 7 of 10 survivors described the circumstances of the overdose occasion as unusual (70%; exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation): 2 injected in places where they had never injected before; 1 used in his own living room, where he had never taken heroin, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply; 2 described unusual injection procedures; 1 took a barbiturate mixture with heroin against his usual practice; 1 injected heroin without the cocaine he usually combined with it, for the first time in over 9 months; 3 of 10 recalled no distinctive feature. Unfamiliar place or company: 3 of 10 (editors' count). No comparison group, no comparison occasions, no test. Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982), as described by its author: rats given a high intravenous heroin dose in the environment previously paired with heroin were more likely to survive than rats with the same history given it in a different environment; no survival figures given. Siegel (2005): no sample size or effect size for any study it cites.

evidence.extracted: The review's account: cues accompanying a drug act as conditional stimuli and its direct effect as the unconditional stimulus; after some pairings the cues elicit compensatory responses that counteract the drug's effect and produce tolerance, which grows as the drug is taken more often. Situational specificity: after repeated doses in one environment, tolerance is apparent there but weakened (the effect partly or completely restored) when the drug is given in a different environment; Fig. 1 is a schematic of this design, not data. The review states that this has been seen for tolerance to a variety of effects, including lethal effects, of various drugs in many species, citing the author's group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure given. Example in rats: rats tolerant to alcohol's temperature-lowering effect showed a rise in body temperature when given an inert substance with alcohol-associated cues.

risk_of_bias.note: The human evidence is a case series (card sc_siegel_1984: JBI prevalence checklist, high risk): 10 survivors from one clinic, chosen in an unreported way, recalling the occasion about 5 years later in open-ended interviews, with the accounts sorted by the author without stated definitions or a second rater; with no comparison occasions and no comparison group, a count of 7 of 10 cannot estimate any risk. The animal work is described by its author without figures (card sc_siegel_2005: a short narrative review of his own research programme, high risk).

inconsistency.note: No conflicting study was read; the author's own data include 3 of 10 who recalled nothing distinctive, which he reads as overdoses with a non-learned basis.

indirectness.note: The evidence that setting changes the chance of dying is from rats; the human study interviewed survivors only, although its abstract extends the idea to deaths, and its unusual circumstances include changes of injection and of drug combination that the rat experiment did not test; the human laboratory examples concern alcohol and caffeine, not opioids or overdose.

imprecision.note: Ten people (7 of 10: exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation) and no comparison against which a risk could be estimated.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the 2005 review cites no study that failed to find setting-specific tolerance.

grade.reasoning: The only human evidence on overdose and setting is a case series of 10 survivors' recollections with no comparison (Siegel, 1984): observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision; very low. The model and the animal findings come from the same author, described without figures in a short narrative review (Siegel, 2005) and in the 1984 paper's introduction; they show why the idea is plausible and are labelled as animal findings, but they are not evidence about people and do not raise the rating. The 1982 rat experiment itself was not read: the PDF saved under its name is a copy of the 1984 paper. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study of people compared overdose occasions with ordinary ones. Status: single study (one human study; the 2005 review adds no human overdose data and does not cite it).

statement: In people with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance treatment in high-income countries, periods out of treatment were associated with higher death rates than periods in treatment, with the highest rates in the first four weeks after leaving; three buprenorphine cohorts showed a similar but less certain pattern. A systematic review pooled 19 cohorts published 1974–2016 (18 methadone cohorts, 122,885 people, followed 1965–2010; 3 buprenorphine cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010; 11 in Europe or Israel, 4 in North America, 4 in Australia), counting time in and out of treatment for the same people (Sordo et al., 2017). With methadone, the pooled all-cause death rate was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years in treatment (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) and 36.1 out of treatment (24.5 to 53.3), an unadjusted difference of 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1) and a ratio of 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86), in 16 cohorts; every cohort had a higher rate out of treatment (cohort rates 5.1 to 39.5 in treatment and 12.4 to 130.2 out). These pooled figures are random-effects averages across very different cohorts (I² 98%): in the three largest, recent register cohorts, which hold 83% of the person-years, the differences were 5.5 to 11.2 and the ratios 1.8 to 2.7, and adding up all deaths and person-years gives 7.1 against 16.4 (editors' calculations from the per-cohort figures). Overdose deaths with methadone (11 cohorts) were 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) in treatment against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out, a difference of 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4) and a ratio of 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96), higher out of treatment in every cohort. By time since starting or leaving methadone (five recent cohorts, after the review left out one cohort of people with HIV who inject; one cohort split at two weeks instead of four), the rate was 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) in the first four weeks of treatment against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) for the rest of treatment, a ratio of 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10) that was not statistically significant; and 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) for the rest of the time out of treatment, a difference of 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3) and a ratio of 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74), higher in the first period in each of the five cohorts; the review did not compare the weeks after leaving with time in treatment directly. The rise after leaving was seen in deaths from all causes: in the three methadone cohorts that gave overdose deaths by period, the overdose rate was 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) later, from 20 overdose deaths in the first period, and in the two cohorts that gave both counts, 18 of the 79 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses (editors' count and calculation); the authors expect overdose deaths to be undercounted and note that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. With buprenorphine (3 cohorts; 96% of the deaths from Australian studies), the rate was 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) in treatment against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4) out (difference 5.2, −1.0 to 11.4; ratio 2.20, 1.34 to 3.61), 4.5 both in the first four weeks and in the rest of treatment, and 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) in the first four weeks after leaving against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9) later (two cohorts; difference 21.2, −5.9 to 48.2). All pooled estimates are unadjusted; in the cohorts that reported ratios adjusted for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment or illness (five methadone and one buprenorphine cohort for all causes), the ratios were unchanged or larger. But people leave and re-enter treatment for reasons that may themselves affect their risk; the review had no data on why people left or on tolerance or drug use after leaving, and its results do not separate people who finished a planned reduction from people who dropped out or were discharged; people lost to follow-up may be at higher risk; medicines obtained outside treatment were not captured; and people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or never treated were excluded. The authors suggest that loss of tolerance, assuming many people return to use, and the use of several substances may explain the rise after leaving. The discussion's statement that death rates were significantly lower with buprenorphine than with methadone has no test or estimate in the results. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Is it dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine? The weeks just after leaving treatment were the riskiest time in these studies. In 16 groups of people on methadone in high-income countries, about 11 in 1,000 died each year while in treatment, against about 36 in 1,000 a year after leaving, and every group had more deaths out of treatment; in the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller, about 6 or 7 a year against 12 to 18. In five groups that split time by weeks, deaths in the first 4 weeks after leaving methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on and about 6 after the first month in treatment. The first month on methadone may also carry more risk (about 11 a year per 1,000 people), but that could be chance. Buprenorphine had only three groups, mostly from one Australian study, with fewer deaths in treatment and a rise after leaving, less certainly. These studies counted everyone who left, for any reason, and could not say why people died: deaths counted as overdoses did not clearly rise after leaving, and nobody recorded tolerance or drug use. People who leave treatment may differ in ways that also affect their risk, so the studies cannot show how much stopping itself raises the risk.
population: People with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance (18 cohorts, 122,885 people, follow-up 1965–2010) or buprenorphine maintenance (3 cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010) in 19 cohorts from high-income countries (11 Europe or Israel, 4 North America, 4 Australia); people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or other treatments, and never-treated people excluded
exposure: Periods out of methadone or buprenorphine maintenance treatment after leaving it, for any reason, with the first four weeks after leaving shown separately; and the first four weeks after starting treatment
comparator: Periods in treatment in the same cohorts (for the interval analyses, the rest of the time in treatment after the first four weeks, and the rest of the time out of treatment after the first four weeks); crude, unadjusted comparisons
outcome: Crude all-cause and overdose death rates per 1,000 person-years, from cohort records and population mortality registers
magnitude: Sordo et al. (2017), pooled crude rates per 1,000 person-years (bivariate random effects; unadjusted). Methadone, all causes (16 cohorts): in treatment 11.3 (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2), out 36.1 (24.5 to 53.3); difference 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1); ratio 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86); I² 98%; cohort rates in 5.1 to 39.5, out 12.4 to 130.2, higher out in all 16; leaving out one cohort at a time 10.6 to 11.9 in and 32.5 to 39.1 out. Editors' calculations from Fig 2: three largest cohorts (Degenhardt 2009, Evans 2015, Kimber 2015; 83% of person-years) differences 8.5, 11.2 and 5.5, ratios 2.5, 2.7 and 1.8; all deaths over all person-years 7.1 in against 16.4 out (ratio 2.3). Methadone, overdose (11 cohorts): 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4); difference 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4); ratio 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96); I² 66% in and 97% out; higher out in all 11 (editors' reading of Fig 3). Methadone by interval (5 cohorts; Degenhardt 2009 split at two weeks): first four weeks in treatment 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) later in treatment, difference 5.6 (−2.4 to 13.6), ratio 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10); first four weeks after leaving 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) later out, difference 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3), ratio 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74); higher in the first period after leaving in each cohort (20.0 against 14.2 to 57.6 against 15.3). Trend analysis: fitted rate falling from 37.4 to 6.4 over the first four weeks of methadone treatment; 24.1 to 35.2 over the first two weeks after leaving, then declining (non-linearity P = 0.04). Overdose by interval, methadone (3 cohorts): in treatment 3.5 (1.3 to 9.5) against 2.0 (1.5 to 2.7); out 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1); 20 overdose deaths in the first four weeks out (editors' count from Fig 6); in Kimber 2015 and Cousins 2016, 10 of 35 and 8 of 44 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses, 18 of 79 (editors' calculation from Figs 4 and 6, same person-years). Buprenorphine, all causes (3 cohorts): 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4); difference 5.2 (−1.0 to 11.4); ratio 2.20 (1.34 to 3.61); by interval (2 cohorts) 4.5 in both treatment periods; first four weeks after leaving 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9), difference 21.2 (−5.9 to 48.2), ratio 2.94 (1.34 to 6.46); overdose (1 cohort) 1.4 against 4.6, and 10.8 against 4.2 out of treatment by interval. Adjusted ratios (Table 4): all causes, methadone, unchanged in two cohorts and 15.5% to 35.5% larger in three; buprenorphine 16.8% larger in one; overdose unchanged in three methadone cohorts and 25.8% and 28.6% larger in two.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the association as worded. The pooled comparisons are crude and the review itself is rated critically low (card sc_sordo_2017: AMSTAR 2, no registered protocol and no list of excluded studies), but the per-cohort data are printed, the direction holds in all 16 cohorts for all causes and all 11 for overdose, adjustment for measured confounders in six cohorts left the ratios unchanged or larger, and the measurement problems the authors name (deaths after a delayed record of leaving counted in treatment; people at higher risk lost to follow-up) would shrink the difference. Time-varying reasons for leaving (relapse, illness, imprisonment) were not measured; they matter for whether stopping treatment causes deaths, which the claim does not say.

inconsistency.note: Rates differ greatly between cohorts (I² 98% for all causes; 66% and 97% for overdose), but every cohort points the same way, and in each of the five cohorts with data by period the first weeks after leaving had a higher rate than later time out of treatment; the statement gives the range and the large-cohort figures.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: people who entered maintenance treatment in high-income countries and left it for any reason; the statement says that planned reductions are not separated from dropping out or discharge, that prison, detoxification and never-treated people were excluded, and that no low- or middle-income country is included.

imprecision.note: The methadone intervals exclude no difference (all causes 13.6 to 36.1; first four weeks after leaving 2.9 to 34.3). The start of methadone treatment and the buprenorphine figures are imprecise (intervals that include no difference, or resting mostly on one Australian cohort) and are worded as uncertain.

publication_bias.note: Some small-study effect for all-cause mortality (extended Egger P = 0.05), attributed by the authors to small cohorts of people with HIV who inject; none for overdose (P = 0.14). Not downgraded: the largest register cohorts show the same direction.

large_effect.note: Not applied (METHODS 6.3): the pooled ratios exceed 2 (3.20 all causes, 4.80 overdose) and adjusted ratios did not shrink, but adjustment was mostly for baseline factors, reasons for leaving that also raise the risk of death could bias away from no difference, and the largest register cohorts show ratios of 1.8 to 2.7.

grade.reasoning: Cohort studies are observational and start low; not downgraded and not upgraded: low for the statement that, in these cohorts, death rates were lower in methadone treatment than out of it and highest in the first four weeks after leaving. A strict reading that downgraded the crude pooled comparisons for unmeasured time-varying confounding would give very low; the claim is worded as an association, gives the unadjusted figures, their size in the largest cohorts and the adjusted results, and is rated for that association. The start of methadone treatment (not statistically significant), the buprenorphine figures (three cohorts, mostly one Australian study), the overdose figures by period (three cohorts, 20 deaths in the key period) and the editors' 18 of 79 are worded as uncertain and not rated separately. Whether treatment prevents deaths, and whether stopping causes them, is not claimed. Status: replicated (16 methadone cohorts from different countries and teams, all in the same direction; the review used non-overlapping years for the two New South Wales cohorts); one review read.

statement: As described in one editorial, with figures second-hand and cases gathered without a search, deaths during opioid withdrawal have been reported, all of them in custody, but the evidence is insufficient to say how often withdrawal leads to death, whether such deaths are increasing, or what the risk is outside custody. The editorial, by three researchers in Sydney, says that opioid withdrawal is generally seen as a flu-like illness, subjectively severe but objectively mild, unlike alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, which it calls life-threatening, and that death is uncommon but does occur (Darke et al., 2017). Its proposed mechanism: persistent vomiting and diarrhoea, if untreated, can lead to dehydration, raised blood sodium (hypernatraemia) and resulting heart failure. Its cases: a woman in custody in the United Kingdom in 1998 who went into heroin withdrawal with persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss and dehydration and died of brain damage from lack of oxygen after a cardiac arrest, a death for which a failure of the duty of care was argued successfully before the European Court of Human Rights; and 10 deaths in United States jails reported in the press between 2013 and 2016 that the authors were aware of (six women and four men, aged 18 to 49), listed in an online appendix that was not read. The authors judge every such death preventable with appropriate medical care, say that in each case the process of dying appeared prolonged, with ample time to treat, and describe the deaths as neglect or a lack of medical resources; they cite one survey in which only a quarter of US jails had alcohol or drug detoxification services. The editorial gives no rate and no number of people going through withdrawal, and its statement that the number of withdrawal deaths in US jails is rising comes without counts over time; the cases come from press reports and a court case, so deaths that were not reported, or not attributed to withdrawal, are missed, and the text does not describe the cases' causes of death beyond the UK case, their medical histories or other drugs involved, including withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Can opioid withdrawal itself kill you? It has happened, but nobody knows how often. Opioid withdrawal is usually seen as awful but not dangerous, unlike alcohol or benzo withdrawal. One editorial lists 11 deaths during opioid withdrawal, all in custody: a woman in the UK in 1998 and 10 people in US jails reported in the press from 2013 to 2016, aged 18 to 49. The authors link these deaths to vomiting and diarrhoea that would not stop and were left untreated, which can dry the body out, raise blood sodium and lead to heart failure. They say each death was slow, with time to treat it, and call them neglect or a lack of medical care. But the list comes from news reports and a court case, not a search, and nobody counted how many people went through withdrawal, so there's no rate, and nothing here covers withdrawal outside custody.
population: People going through opioid withdrawal in custody (jails and prisons in the United Kingdom and the United States), as described in one editorial
exposure: Opioid withdrawal (from heroin and other opioids) without adequate medical management
comparator: None (reported cases; no comparison group and no denominator)
outcome: Death during withdrawal, as reported in the press and in a court case (causes as the editorial gives them)
magnitude: No rate or denominator. Darke et al. (2017), second-hand: 1 death in UK custody (1998); 10 press-reported deaths in US jails, 2013–2016 (6 women, 4 men, aged 18 to 49; listed in an appendix not read). Second-hand figure: a quarter of US jails in one survey (Fiscella et al., 2004) had alcohol or drug detoxification services.
